title: Cabinet Approves Rs 52,878 Crore IDBI Bank Sale to Fairfax Arm
excerpt: The CCEA cleared Fairfax subsidiary 10955230 Canada Inc. to buy 60.72% of IDBI Bank at Rs 81 per share, in what ministers called India's largest financial-sector FDI.
body:
• The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved the sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank to 10955230 Canada Inc., a subsidiary of Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings, for Rs 52,878 crore at Rs 81 per share.
  • The government will sell 30.48% and Life Insurance Corporation of India will sell 30.24%; they will retain 15% and 19% respectively, down from 45.48% and 49.24% before the deal.
  • Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw called the transaction India's largest foreign direct investment in the financial sector; completion is expected by March 2027.
  • For IDBI depositors and borrowers, nothing changes on day one: this is a transfer of existing shares, not a merger or closure, and the bank remains RBI-regulated. Shareholders should note the Rs 81 deal price sits below the recent market price.

India's Cabinet has approved the sale of a controlling stake in IDBI Bank to a Fairfax Financial Holdings subsidiary for Rs 52,878 crore, clearing the largest foreign direct investment in the country's financial sector and ending a sale process that has run for more than a decade.

The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved 10955230 Canada Inc. — the Fairfax arm led by Indian-Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa — as strategic buyer on October 14, according to a Finance Ministry statement reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw described the transaction as India's largest foreign direct investment in the financial sector.

How the Sale Is Structured

The mechanism is a secondary share transfer, not a fresh issue of capital. Fairfax's Canadian subsidiary will buy existing shares from the bank's two public-sector owners: 30.48% from the Government of India and 30.24% from the state-run Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), The Rs 52,878 crore consideration therefore flows to the government and LIC as sellers, rather than onto IDBI Bank's own balance sheet as new capital.

At Rs 81, the winning bid sits above the Rs 75.99 benchmark price — the average of two independent valuations used to evaluate revised bids — but well below the Rs 94.42 reserve price the government had set earlier. After completion, the government will hold 15% and LIC 19%, a combined 34%, and both will cease to be promoters in control of the bank. IDBI is already classified officially as a private-sector bank, so the government has framed the transaction as a change of control rather than a conventional privatisation.

"It is not a disinvestment, but a restructuring. This is because the government will remain invested in IDBI Bank."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister

Why the Shares Fell After Approval

The market's first verdict was on price, not strategy. IDBI Bank shares surged about 9% on October 14 ahead of the announcement, closing at Rs 90.40, then fell more than 7% the next day to around Rs 84, according to Outlook Business. At Rs 81, Fairfax's price is a discount of about 10.4% to that close — above the government's valuation benchmark, but below what investors had just paid in the open market.

A Sale a Decade in the Making

The formal disinvestment process began in October 2022. It stalled earlier this year when initial financial bids in FY26 came in below the Rs 94.42 per share reserve price and were rejected, forcing the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management to invite fresh sealed bids from qualified bidders against the lower Rs 75.99 benchmark. Mint noted in its editorial assessment of the deal that the sale revives the disinvestment programme: the Centre has raised Rs 55,757 crore in 2026-27 against an Rs 80,000 crore target, and its IDBI proceeds would push receipts toward that goal.

Conditions Fairfax Must Meet

Cabinet approval is not completion. The buyer must present its credentials to the Reserve Bank of India under the fit-and-proper assessment from the expression-of-interest stage and submit a roadmap for meeting regulatory conditions, the Finance Ministry statement said. Reported conditions include retaining the IDBI Bank name for three years, a five-year lock-in on Fairfax's capital, and reducing its holding to 26% over 15 years on a timeline agreed with the RBI — the standard dilution path for Indian bank promoters. LIC must bring its residual stake from about 19% to 15% within two years of completion, and the government may sell its remaining 15% through the open market.

Fairfax also faces a two-bank problem. Through FIH Mauritius Investments it owns about 40% of Kerala-based CSB Bank, and RBI rules bar one promoter from controlling two banks. Fairfax must decide within two years whether to merge CSB with IDBI or reduce its CSB holding.

What Happens Next

Completion is expected by March 2027. Before then, investors will watch for the RBI's fit-and-proper clearance, Fairfax's compliance roadmap, and its decision on CSB Bank.
